score_comment_short: Ownership is visible, but the work's size and results stay mostly unmeasured.
score_comment_long: The launch and onboarding lines show you coordinating work across teams. The quarterly roadmap landing on time gives one concrete result. Add the missing team, volume, and before-and-after details to show how much changed.
first_impression: Cross-team launch ownership stands out first, especially the clear owners and checkpoints. The resume still leaves recruiters guessing about team size, program volume, and what improved.
score_plain: This should earn a closer read for Program Manager roles. It may lose stronger matches when recruiters cannot size the work.
biggest_gap_example: 'Led onboarding work across the company, improving productivity.' names no team, volume, or productivity measure, so recruiters cannot size the result.
summary: Cross-team launches are the clearest thread in your Program Manager experience. You keep work moving through clear owners, checkpoints, stakeholder alignment, and a quarterly roadmap delivered on time. That makes day-to-day ownership believable. How many teams or people were involved, and what changed after the work? Until those facts are visible, the resume stops short of a senior-level first read.
strengths: The launch bullet names clear owners and checkpoints, so the way you coordinate work is easy to follow.
Delivering the quarterly roadmap on time gives recruiters one concrete result to hold onto.
Onboarding, launches, and stakeholder alignment form a consistent Program Manager story.
gaps: The onboarding line never names the teams, weekly volume, or the specific productivity change, so its scale is impossible to judge.
The launch line explains the process but stops before the result, leaving its business value unanswered.
Without a summary, recruiters must infer whether you are targeting program management, product operations, or core product work.
